title.en: Maeldun's Birth and the Boat of the Druid's Rule
title.zh: 梅爾敦的誕生與德魯伊法則之舟

region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋郡阿倫群島

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin, Book of the Dun Cow recension), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle of the Owenacht of Aran is slain by reavers who burn the church of Doocloone over him, and a son is born who is reared as the queen's own — beautiful beyond flesh, out-throwing every boy at ball and stone. Taunted with not knowing his kindred, Maeldun fasts till his mother is found, learns his father's ashes lie under the scorched flagstone where he was casting the stone, and builds a coracle of skins threefold at a Druid's word: seventeen men only, on the days the wizard names — and the three foster-brothers who swim after the boat bring on them all the punishment of a transgressed rule.
summary.zh: 阿倫群島「戰刃埃利爾」遭萊克斯海寇焚教堂殺害；其遺腹子梅爾敦由王后撫養，俊美非凡、擲石賽跑冠絕同儕。因人嘲其不知親族，他絕食探母；最終得知父親骨灰正埋於他擲石而立的焦黑石板之下。他依德魯伊之言製三層皮革小舟：僅限十七人同行——而三名跳海追舟的乳兄弟，卻為全體招來觸犯法則的懲罰。

sensitivity.note: The voyage of Maeldun is the oldest Irish wonder-voyage (model for St Brendan's); the Druid's fixed rule (seventeen men, named days) and the transgression by the foster-brothers set the penance-frame of the whole immram — the tale teaches 'the oracular injunctions of wizards should be obeyed', as Rolleston notes, but it is Christian-era mythology built on pagan sea-quest stock. Pin is the real Aran Islands.

passages.text: One day a proud young warrior who had been defeated by him taunted him with his lack of knowledge of his kindred and descent. Maeldun went to his foster-mother, the queen, and said: "I will not eat nor drink till thou tell me who are my mother and my father." The queen at last took him to his own mother, the nun, who told him: "Thy father was Ailill of the Owens of Aran." Then Maeldun went to his own kindred, and was well received by them. After a time Maeldun happened to be among a company of young warriors who were contending at putting the stone in the graveyard of the ruined church of Doocloone; Maeldun's foot was planted, as he heaved the stone, on a scorched and blackened flagstone; and one who was by, a monk named Briccne, said to him: "It were better for thee to avenge the man who was burnt there than to cast stones over his burnt bones." "Who was that?" "Ailill, thy father." "Who slew him?" "Reavers from Leix."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Maeldun threw down the stone he was about to cast, and put his mantle round him and went home. At the advice of a Druid he then built him a boat, or coracle, of skins lapped threefold one over the other; and the wizard also told him that seventeen men only must accompany him, and on what day he must begin the boat and on what day he must put out to sea. So when his company was ready he put out and hoisted the sail, but had gone only a little way when his three foster-brothers came down to the beach and entreated him to take them. "Get you home, for none but the number I have may go with me." But the three youths would not be separated from Maeldun, and they flung themselves into the sea. He turned back, lest they should be drowned, and brought them into his boat; and all were punished for this transgression, and Maeldun condemned to wandering until expiation had been made.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Slaves and the Wind of Punishment

region.en: Two bare islands of the western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海兩座荒島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Rowing all day and half the night, the voyagers come to two small bare islands with two forts, and hear armed men quarrelling: 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me.' Maeldun is about to land for vengeance, but a great wind arises suddenly and blows them off into the boundless ocean — 'Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid' — and vengeance itself is postponed by the penalty of the broken rule.
summary.zh: 晝夜划行後，他們抵達兩座荒島，聽見武裝者的爭吵：「正是我殺了戰刃埃利爾、焚其教堂，至今無族人復仇。」梅爾敦欲登岸復仇，狂風驟起，將小舟吹入無垠大洋——「是你們違德魯伊之言擅自登舟，招此懲罰。」復仇因破誓之罰而延宕。

sensitivity.note: The wind that blows the avenger away from his vengeance is the immram's fixed moral device — the quest is penance, not reprisal; the two fort islands parallel the twin-fort openings of voyage literature (cf. the Coire Brecain twin isles). Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Maeldun and his crew had rowed all day and half the night when they came to two small bare islands with two forts in them, and a noise was heard from them of armed men quarrelling. "Stand off from me, for I am a better man than thou. 'Twas I slew Ailill of the Edge-of-Battle and burned the church of Doocloone over him, and no kinsman has avenged his death on me. And thou hast never done the like of that."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Maeldun was about to land, and German and Diuran the Rhymer cried that God had guided them to the spot where they would be. But a great wind arose suddenly and blew them off into the boundless ocean, and Maeldun said to his foster-brothers: "Ye have caused this to be, casting yourselves on board in spite of the words of the Druid." And they had no answer, save only to be silent for a little space.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Cat and the Necklace of Ashes

region.en: Tower island of the white houses (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白屋高塔之島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Hungry and thirsting, they reach a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and enter the great house where no man is — only a little cat playing on four stone pillars, leaping from one to the other; on the walls hang three rows of brooches, neck-torques as big as cask-hoops, and great swords with gold and silver hilts, and a roasted ox with abundance of liquor lies ready. They eat and sleep; and next morning the youngest foster-brother takes a necklace from the wall — and the cat leaps through him like a fiery arrow, and he falls a heap of ashes.
summary.zh: 飢渴交加之際，他們登上一座直插雲霄的白堊高塔之島；大屋中無人，唯有一隻小貓在四根石柱間跳躍嬉戲；牆上掛著三排金銀胸針、桶箍般大的金銀項圈與金柄寶劍，烤牛與美酒已備。他們飽食安睡；翌晨最年輕的乳兄弟竟從牆上取走項鍊——小貓如烈焰之箭穿身而過，他倒地化為一堆灰燼。

sensitivity.note: The cat that leaps 'like a fiery arrow' is the fixed guardian-sprite of the immram's wonder-houses (the Island of the Little Cat is the voyage's most famous theft-punishment); hospitality taken freely but a jewel stolen = death — a clean moral of otherworld property. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: This was, as it were, a tall white tower of chalk reaching up to the clouds, and on the rampart about it were great houses white as snow. They entered the largest of them, and found no man in it, but a small cat playing on four stone pillars which were in the midst of the house, leaping from one to the other. It looked a little on the Irish warriors, but did not cease from its play. On the walls of the houses there were three rows of objects hanging up, one row of brooches of gold and silver, and one of neck-torques of gold and silver, each as big as the hoop of a cask, and one of great swords with gold and silver hilts. Quilts and shining garments lay in the room, and there, also, were a roasted ox and a flitch of bacon and abundance of liquor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Hath this been left for us?" said Maeldun to the cat. It looked at him a moment, and then continued its play. So there they ate and drank and slept, and stored up what remained of the food. Next day, as they made to leave the house, the youngest of Maeldun's foster-brothers took a necklace from the wall, and was bearing it out when the cat suddenly "leaped through him like a fiery arrow," and he fell, a heap of ashes, on the floor. Thereupon Maeldun, who had forbidden the theft of the jewel, soothed the cat and replaced the necklace, and they strewed the ashes of the dead youth on the sea-shore, and put to sea again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mill That Grinds Men's Grudges

region.en: Island of the Mill, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西海巨磨之島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: They find a great and grim-looking mill, and a giant miller grinding corn in it: 'Half the corn of your country is ground here. Here comes to be ground all that men begrudge to each other.' Heavy and many are the loads going to it, and all that is ground in it is carried away westwards — so they cross themselves and sail away. It is the voyage's clearest allegory, the sea-mill of envy standing where in later Irish sea-lore the whirlpool Corryvreckan turns.
summary.zh: 他們見到一座猙獰巨磨，巨人磨坊主正在磨穀：「爾國之穀，半數在此研磨；凡人間互相嫉恨之物，皆運至此研磨。」沉重的穀物源源運來，磨成之物皆向西流去——眾人畫十字而速去。此乃航程中最直白的寓意之島：嫉妒之海磨，正是後世愛爾蘭海傳說中迴漩的科里弗雷坎漩渦。

sensitivity.note: The grudge-mill is the immram's moral allegory (traditionally located at the whirlpool of Corryvreckan); the westward drift of what is ground away is the Irish eschatological geography (all rivers run west to the otherworld). Tagged 'world-renewal' for the sea-as-purgation reading, interpretive.

passages.text: Here they found a great and grim-looking mill, and a giant miller grinding corn in it. "Half the corn of your country," he said, "is ground here. Here comes to be ground all that men begrudge to each other."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Heavy and many were the loads they saw going to it, and all that was ground in it was carried away westwards. So they crossed themselves and sailed away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Silvern Column and the Mesh of the Net

region.en: Sea of the silvern column (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白銀巨柱之海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: One of the most striking episodes of the voyage: a great silvern column, four-square, rising from the boundless ocean, its summit lost in the sky, and from that summit a huge silver net flung far away into the sea. Through a mesh of the net they sail — and Diuran hacks away a piece of it: 'Destroy it not, for what we see is the work of mighty men.' 'For the praise of God's name I do this, that our tale may be believed; if I reach Ireland again, this silver shall be offered on the high altar of Armagh.' Two ounces and a half it weighed, measured afterwards in Armagh.
summary.zh: 航程最壯麗的一幕：四方白銀巨柱自無垠大洋拔海而起，柱頂沒入天際，一張巨大銀網自柱頂遠拋入海。眾人自網眼間駛過——狄烏蘭竟砍下一片：「勿毀之！此乃偉人所造。」「我以此榮耀神名，使我等傳說可信；若得歸國，此銀必供於阿馬大祭壇。」該銀片後在阿馬秤得二盎斯半。

sensitivity.note: The silvern column with its net is the immram's most abstract revelation-image (a cosmic fishing of the world); the relic taken for proof — weighed in Armagh — is the voyage's Christian-world verification device, unique among the islands. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was a great silvern column, four-square, rising from the sea. Each of its four sides was as wide as two oar-strokes of the boat. Not a sod of earth was at its foot, but it rose from the boundless ocean and its summit was lost in the sky. From that summit a huge silver net was flung far away into the sea, and through a mesh of that net they sailed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they did so Diuran hacked away a piece of the net. "Destroy it not," said Maeldun, "for what we see is the work of mighty men." Diuran said: "For the praise of God's name I do this, that our tale may be believed, and if I reach Ireland again this piece of silver shall be offered by me on the high altar of Armagh." Two ounces and a half it weighed when it was measured afterwards in Armagh. And then they heard a voice from the summit of yonder pillar, mighty, clear, and distinct; but they knew not the tongue it spake, or the words it uttered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Island of the Women and the Clue of Twine

region.en: Dun of the seventeen maidens (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 十七少女的堡壘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Voyage of Maeldun (Imram Maelduin), retold in T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911)

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), ch. VII, eBook #34630

summary.en: Within a mighty dun, seventeen maidens prepare a great bath; a rider richly clad comes up on a racehorse and is seen to be a woman — the queen. Maeldun is wedded to her, each of his men to a maiden, and she promises that old age will never fall on them if they stay. But the men weary — three months were three years — and put to sea while she is away judging the folk; she comes riding with a clew of twine and flings it, and it clings to Maeldun's hand so that he cannot free himself. So next time another man catches it, and Diuran smites off his hand, and it falls with the clew into the sea; and all the land was one cry of wailing as they escaped.
summary.zh: 宏偉堡壘內，十七位少女正備浴；一名衣飾華美的騎手乘賽馬而至——竟是女王。梅爾敦娶她為妻，部眾各配一女；她許諾：留此則永駐青春。然三月如三年，眾人思歸，趁女王出巡登舟而逃；她持絲線馳至擲出，線竟黏在梅爾敦掌上不能脫。下次由另一人接線，狄烏蘭揮劍斷其手，線與手俱落海中——全島哭聲震野，他們終於逃出女人島。

sensitivity.note: The queen's clew that clings is the binding-token motif (compare the ball of thread at the Land of Women in the Bran voyage — the two tales share the device); three months that are three years is the otherworld-time rule. Note the self-mutilation for escape is documented in the source. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: They landed to look on it, and sat on a hillock near by. Within the dun they saw seventeen maidens busy at preparing a great bath. In a little while a rider, richly clad, came up swiftly on a racehorse, and lighted down and went inside... And Maeldun was wedded to the queen, and each of the maidens to one of his men. "Stay here, and old age will never fall on you, but ye shall remain as ye are now for ever and ever... So they remained there for three months of winter; but at the end of that time it seemed they had been there three years, and the men wearied of it, and longed to set forth for their own country.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: But before they had gone far the queen came riding up with a clew of twine in her hand, and she flung it after them. Maeldun caught it in his hand, and it clung to his hand so that he could not free himself, and the queen, holding the other end, drew them back to land. Twice again the same thing happened, and the next time another man caught the clew, but it clung to his hand as before; so Diuran smote off his hand, and it fell with the clew into the sea. "When she saw that she at once began to wail and shriek, so that all the land was one cry, wailing and shrieking." And thus they escaped from the Island of the Women.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911, ch. VII; not verbatim.
